analysis.one_liner: Cuts brand-name biologic drug monopolies from 12 years to 5 years so cheaper copies arrive sooner.
analysis.headline: The bill to shorten biologic drug exclusivity from 12 to 5 years drew 22 cosponsors but never left the House Energy and Commerce Committee before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Biologic drugs are advanced medicines made from living cells, and brand-name makers currently get 12 years of exclusive sales before competitors can sell cheaper near-identical copies, called biosimilars. This bill would cut that monopoly window to 5 years, letting biosimilar makers enter the market sooner and push prices down. It would apply only to brand-name biologics approved after the bill became law, so existing drugs would keep their current exclusivity.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take biologic drugs, which include treatments for arthritis, cancer, diabetes, and autoimmune diseases, would gain access to cheaper biosimilar versions years earlier. Insurers and employers who pay drug bills would also save, and taxpayers would pay less through Medicare and Medicaid. Biosimilar manufacturers would gain an earlier market opening.

how_it_helps.text: Shortens the marketing exclusivity period for brand-name biological products from 12 years to 5 years under the Public Health Service Act [S3].
Allows biosimilars to be marketed five years after the reference brand-name biological product is licensed, instead of twelve [S2].
Conforming amendments reduce the related exclusivity periods in the biosimilar approval pathway from 12 years to 5 years, so competitors can actually reach the market at year five [S3].
Applies only to brand-name biologics licensed on or after enactment, so no existing drug loses any of its current exclusivity period [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic makers would lose up to seven years of monopoly sales on new drugs, during which they charge prices no generic-style competitor can match. Biotech investors who fund drug development on the expectation of long exclusivity would face a shorter runway to recoup investment. Patients would pay nothing directly; they gain.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection, widely raised by the biotech industry in exclusivity debates, is that biologics are far costlier and riskier to develop than ordinary pills, and cutting exclusivity from 12 to 5 years could reduce investment in new biologic medicines. This argument is not in the provided record, so it rests on general knowledge of the standard industry position, not on this bill's file.

The bill would do nothing for prices already being paid, because it applies only to brand-name biologics licensed after enactment, so any price relief would be years away even if it had become law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but deferred: faster biosimilar competition has historically brought steep price cuts, and no existing drug would lose protection. The cost falls entirely on brand-name drug makers' future profits, with a credible but contested concern that weaker exclusivity could blunt investment in new biologics. On balance the trade is strongly favorable to consumers, and the main reason it did not happen was political, not substantive.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee in June 2019, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended in January 2021 [S5].

narrative.text: Introduced on June 20, 2019 by Rep. Janice Schakowsky with 16 original cosponsors, including one Republican, Rep. Bruce Westerman [S1].
Referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].

Referred the next day to the Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed; the complete action history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action at any point through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].
It picked up 22 cosponsors in total, 21 Democrats and 1 Republican [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic manufacturers kept the 12-year monopoly structure on new drugs, and nothing changed for patients' drug prices. The committee leadership that never scheduled action faced no consequence for leaving it there.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 16 original cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 20, 2019 and never reported the bill out; the full action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote [S5].

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee under his chairmanship never scheduled the bill for subcommittee or full-committee action, so it died at the referral stage.

sides.party_line_note: Support was nearly all Democratic: 21 of the 22 cosponsors were House Democrats, with a single Republican, Rep. Bruce Westerman [S4].

industries.note: The bill would cut their exclusive-sales window on new biologic drugs from 12 years to 5, ending years in which they can set prices without biosimilar competition. Patients currently paying monopoly prices for biologics bear the cost of that extended exclusivity.
A shorter exclusivity period opens the market to their cheaper versions seven years sooner, which lowers costs for patients and payers at the same time.

A shorter monopoly window shrinks the expected returns on new biologic development, which is the core argument for the current 12-year period; whether that materially slows new medicines is contested.
